$comment: Topic maps for scripts/gap-audit.py. Each topic groups themes; each theme
groups concepts. A concept declares `terms` (lexical probes run against the
index), an optional `probe` sentence (used by --semantic), and `canonical`
works that would close the gap if the verdict comes back absent/mention-only.
Keep terms specific: generic words ('time', 'change', 'identity') match

And does it cover the mismatch between the philosophical and the data-engineering traditions?

process-simulation.title: Process simulation — data-driven BPS, discrete-event simulation and queueing
process-simulation.question: Van der Aalst's 31-10-2025 deck argues that classical queueing assumptions are the wrong model for a business process, that no process is in steady state, and that the way forward is short-term simulation amalgamated with machine learning. Does the collection hold the literature those claims are made against — the queueing theory, the discrete-event simulation methodology, the queue-mining line — or only the process-mining papers that cite them?

artifact-centric-simulation.title: Artifact-centric & declarative process models — can they be simulated the way BPMN is?
artifact-centric-simulation.question: Business process simulation is an imperative-model discipline: a BPS model is a BPMN model or a Petri net plus branching probabilities, durations and an arrival process, and the engine plays the token game. Artifact-centric models (Nigam & Caswell's business artifacts, Hull's Guard-Stage-Milestone) and the declarative languages beside them (Declare, DCR, CMMN) have no token game — behaviour is whatever satisfies the constraints. So does the collection hold the literature on *analysing* these models quantitatively, and does that literature even exist? The four candidate answers the field actually gives are enactment, verification, constraint-based log generation, and the object-centric turn; this map audits each separately, so a MISSING verdict distinguishes a hole in the library from a hole in the research.

themes.name: Simulating a declarative model — log generation is the operative form
themes.note: This is the closest thing to an answer, and the crux of the whole question. A declarative model cannot be played forward token-by-token, so 'simulation' means *sampling from the set of traces satisfying the constraints* — via automata, SAT/Alloy, or ASP. Note what these tools do not produce: timestamps drawn from distributions, resources, or queues. They generate behaviour, not performance.

timeseries-process-mining.title: Time-series data mining × process mining — representation, motifs, anomalies, forecasting and counterfactuals
timeseries-process-mining.question: The internal Supply Chain / Ontology / AI summit asks the PIG to hold time series data as a first-class object type rather than through 'helper objects', to time-version every node and link attribute, to answer Inventory(now) / Inventory(yesterday) / Inventory(future) through one query interface 'leveraging different models for projection', to derive statistical distributions from data as the base for simulation, to carry an Occurrence_Probability and an Impact_Distribution on an InfluenceLink, and to infer rules from timestamps ('people don't do X on Sundays'). Does the collection hold the time-series data-mining literature those requirements land in — representation and indexing, motif and discord discovery, anomaly detection and its benchmark critique, forecasting and imputation, counterfactual estimation, and the storage engines underneath — or only the process-mining papers that mention time series in passing?

themes.name: Representation, indexing and similarity
themes.note: Keogh's foundational layer: before anything can be mined, a series has to be represented and compared. This is the most-cited body of work in the field and the part a semantic layer would have to choose from when it decides how a stock-history object type is stored and searched.
